<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par88" />the Aramaic {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁמְרַ֫יִן}} = {{GHGheb|text=שָֽׁמְרָן}} for the Hebrew {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁמְרוֹן|translate=Samaria}}.—We may add to this list {{GHGheb|text=אֶפְרַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=נַֽהֲרַ֫יִם|translate=the river country}} (in the Tel-el-Amarna letters ''nârima, naʾrima''), {{GHGheb|text=מִצְרַ֫יִם|translate=Egypt}}, Phoenician {{GHGheb|text=מצרם}}; also the words denoting time, {{GHGheb|text=צָֽהֳרַ֫יִם|translate=midday}} (Mêšaʿ inscription, line 15 {{GHGheb|text=צהרם}}), and perhaps {{GHGheb|text=עַרְבַּ֫יִם|translate=in the evening}}, if the regular expression {{GHGheb|text=בֵּין־הָֽעַרְבַּ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, &c., is only due to mistaking {{GHGheb|text=עַרְבַּ֫יִם}} for a dual: LXX πρὸς ἑσπέραν, τὸ δειλινόν, ὀψέ and only in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=23|verse=5}} ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν ἑσπερινῶν. The Arabs also say ''el ʿišâʾân'', ''the two evenings'', cf. Kuhn’s ''Literaturblatt'', iii. 48.

Instead of the supposed dual {{GHGheb|text=יָדַי}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=13|verse=18}} read {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם}}. On {{GHGheb|text=חַלּוֹנַי}} (generally taken to be ''a double window'') {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=22|verse=14}}, see above, {{GHGpar|87|g}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|d}}
2. Only apparently dual-forms (but really plural) are the words {{GHGheb|text=מַ֫יִם|translate=water}} and {{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַ֫יִם|translate=heaven}}. According to P. Haupt in {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} (critical notes on Isaiah, p. 157, line 18 ff.), they are to be derived from the old plural forms (found in Assyrian) ''mâmi'', ''šamâmi'', whence the Hebr. {{GHGheb|text=מים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שמים}} arose by inversion of the ''i'', ''mâmi, mâimi, maim''. It is simpler, however, to suppose that the primitive singulars ''may'' and ''šamay'', when they took the plural of extension ({{GHGpar|124|b}}), kept the tone on the ''ay'', thus causing the ''îm'' (which otherwise always has the tone, {{GHGpar|87|a}}) to be shortened to ''im''. Cf. the analogous formations, Arab. ''tarḍaina'', ''2nd fem. sing. imperf''. of a verb {{GHGheb|text=ל״י}}, for ''tarḍay'' + ''îna'', corresponding to ''taqtulîna'' in the strong verb; also bibl.-Aram. {{GHGheb|text=בָּנַ֫יִן}} the ''abs. st. plur''. of the ''ptcp. Qal'' of {{GHGheb|text=(ל״י) בְּנָה}}, which otherwise always ends in ''în'' with the tone, e.g. in the ''ptcp. Qal'' of the strong verb, {{GHGheb|text=דָּֽבְחִין|translate=sacrificing}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|e}}
'''2.''' The use of the dual in Hebrew is confined, except in the numerals 2, 12, 200, &c. (see {{GHGpar|97}}), practically to those objects which are by nature or art always found in ''pairs'', especially to the double members of the body (but not necessarily so, cf. {{GHGheb|text=זְרֹעִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=זְרֹעוֹת|translate=arms}}, never in the dual), e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָדַ֫יִם|translate=both hands}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָזְנַ֫יִם|translate=both ears}}, {{GHGheb|text=שִׁנַּ֫יִם|translate=teeth}} (of both rows), also {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲלַ֫יִם|translate=a pair of sandals}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֹֽאזְנַ֫יִם|translate=a pair of scales}}, Lat. ''bilanx'', &c.; or things which are at least thought of as forming a pair, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יוֹמַ֫יִם|translate=two}} (successive) ''days'', Lat. ''biduum''; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבֻעַ֫יִם|translate=two weeks}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנָתַ֫יִם|translate=two years}} (in succession), Lat. ''biennium''; {{GHGheb|text=אַמָּתַ֫יִם|translate=two cubits}}.<ref>But for {{GHGheb|text=דְּרָכַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=28|verse=6.18}} (which the Masora takes as two roads leading from the cross-ways) {{GHGheb|text=דְּרָכִים}} is to be read.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|f}}
In the former case the dual may be used for a plural, either indefinite or defined by a numeral, where it is thought of in a double arrangement, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אַרְבַּע רַגְלָ֑יִם|translate=four feet}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=11|verse=23}}; {{GHGheb|text=שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַ֫יִם|translate=six wings}} (i.e. three pairs), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=1|verse=6}}; even {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָה עֵינַ֫יִם|translate=seven eyes}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־בִּרְכַּ֫יִם|translate=all knees}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=7|verse=17}}; {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־יָדַ֫יִם|translate=all hands}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=21|verse=12}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְצִלְתַּ֫יִם|translate=cymbals}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=3|verse=10}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁפַתַּ֫יִם|translate=double-hooks}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=40|verse=43}}.—To express a certain emphasis the numeral ''two'' is used with the dual, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=16|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=12}}.—See some other remarks on the use of the dual in {{GHGpar|87|o}} and s.

{{GHGmargin-letter|88|g}}
It is not impossible that Hebrew at an earlier period made a more extensive and freer use of the dual, and that the restrictions and limitations of its use, mentioned above, belong to a relatively later phase of development. The<section end="par88" /><noinclude>
